```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.align = "center",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This guide extends the introductory vignette (`vignettes/FLicc_intro_vignette.Rmd`).
It walks through a complete assessment with the built-in splendid alfonsino data,
with explicit **checks** at each step (what to look at, what is a red flag, what
to do about it), and documents the options added in FLicc 1.0.9 and 1.0.10:
fishing mortality over time, effective sample size, missing data, tail
treatment, reference points with steepness, length-based indicators,
Monte-Carlo ensembles and use inside an MSE. Recommendations marked
*simulation* come from tests with an alfonsino-like operating model
(fixed-CV length-at-age, annual recruitment, Beverton-Holt h = 0.75, two gears,
two-stage length sampling).

# Installation

`FLicc` depends on `FLCore`, `ggplotFL` and `TMB`. On Windows, compiling the TMB
model requires Rtools (<https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/>).

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("TMB", type = "source")
install.packages(c("FLCore", "ggplotFL"),
                 repos = c("https://flr.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
remotes::install_github("henning-winker/FLicc")                    # release
remotes::install_github("henning-winker/FLicc", ref = "dev-merge")  # development
```

```{r load}
library(FLicc)
packageVersion("FLicc")
```

# Workflow and defaults

1. **Data**: length frequencies by gear as `FLQuants`; check sample sizes, gaps and the tail.
2. **Effective sample size**: rescale the counts to the information they carry.
3. **Life history**: `FLPar` and `stocklen()`; check Linf against the largest fish.
4. **Fit**: `fiticc()`; check convergence, residuals, selectivity and retrospective consistency.
5. **Status**: SPR, Fspr, steepness-corrected biomass, length-based indicators.
6. **Uncertainty**: life-history ensembles with `mc_flicc()`; sensitivity runs.
7. **Management**: `flicc.sa()` and harvest control rules in an MSE.

A plain `fiticc()` call uses the GTG population model, a multinomial likelihood,
fixed growth (Linf, CVL) and natural mortality, and a random walk on log F with
its standard deviation fixed at `sigmaF = 0.3`. These defaults are fast and
stable; every other option is a deliberate change.

# Length-frequency data

## Structure

```{r data}
data("alfonsino")
lfd <- FLQuantLen(lfd_long_to_wide(as.data.frame(lfd_alfonsino)), unit = "cm", midL = FALSE)
names(lfd)
range(as.numeric(dimnames(lfd[[1]])$len)); range(as.numeric(dimnames(lfd[[1]])$year))
```

`FLQuantLen()` takes a wide table (`lfd_long_to_wide()` converts a long one) with
columns for length, year, gear and counts; `midL = FALSE` means lengths are lower
bin boundaries. Bins must be equally spaced and identical across gears and years
(`complete_lfd_bins()` fills gaps with zeros).

## Check 1: sample size by year and gear

```{r check-n, fig.height = 5}
plot_lfdn(lfd)
```

| | |
|---|---|
| **Why** | The information in a composition depends on how many independent samples (trips, hauls, landings) it comes from, not only on the number of fish. |
| **Look for** | Gear-years with very few fish or few occupied bins (labels), years where one gear is missing, strong changes in the gear mix between years. |
| **Red flags** | Gear-years with < 50 fish or < 10 occupied bins; a gear present only in some years; combined sample size dominated by one gear in some years and another in others. |
| **Action** | Set effective sample sizes per gear (section 4); consider dropping or pooling very poor gear-years; check that `catch_by_gear` reflects the catch, not the sampling, split. |

## Check 2: consistency of the compositions

```{r check-lfd, fig.height = 5}
plot_lfd(lfd, type = "relmax")
```

| | |
|---|---|
| **Look for** | Stable shapes and modes between adjacent years; similar left limbs within a gear (selectivity is assumed constant over time). |
| **Red flags** | Abrupt shifts in the mode or left limb (change of gear, mesh, market sorting or sampling programme); bimodal compositions from mixing gears or areas; truncation at the right (size limits, sorting). |
| **Action** | Split gears or periods with different selectivity; restrict `years`; investigate sampling before modelling around it. |

## Check 3: the largest fish

```{r check-tail}
linf_in <- 55.7
sapply(lfd, function(x) {
  L <- as.numeric(dimnames(x)$len); n <- apply(x@.Data, 1, sum)
  c(max_length = max(L[n > 0]), pct_ge_0.9Linf = round(100 * sum(n[L >= 0.9 * linf_in]) / sum(n), 1),
    pct_ge_Linf = round(100 * sum(n[L >= linf_in]) / sum(n), 2))
})
```

| | |
|---|---|
| **Why** | The tail is the part of the composition most sensitive to Linf, CVL, dome-shaped selectivity and the GTG discretisation. |
| **Red flags** | More than about 1% of fish at or above the input Linf; a long thin tail far beyond Linf (misidentified species, measurement errors, other stocks). |
| **Action** | Re-examine Linf; use a tail cut (section 11) or `rob_eps`; `tail_warning = TRUE` in `settings` reports fish beyond the largest growth group. |

## Check 4: empirical catch curves

A log-linear catch curve on the length-converted ages gives a quick, model-free
view of total mortality by year and of its trend:

```{r check-zlcc, fig.height = 5}
lhpar <- FLPar(linf = 55.7, k = 0.08, M = 0.162, L50 = 31.1859,
               a = 0.004721956 / 1000, b = 3.146168)
plot_zlcc(lfd$Trawl, lhpar)
```

| | |
|---|---|
| **Look for** | Roughly linear descending limbs; a stable or smoothly changing slope (Z). |
| **Red flags** | Strongly curved descending limbs (dome-shaped selectivity, recruitment pulses), slopes jumping between years (sampling noise or changing selectivity). |
| **Action** | Consider `dsnormal` selectivity or a tail cut; expect noisy annual F and keep the random walk. |

# Effective sample size

## How the sample size enters the likelihood

For gear $g$ in year $y$, with observed counts $y_{g,y,l}$, total
$n_{g,y} = \sum_l y_{g,y,l}$ and predicted proportions $\pi_{g,y,l}$:

- **Multinomial** (`obs_model = "mn"`): $-\log L = -\sum_l y_{g,y,l} \log \pi_{g,y,l}$.
  The weight of a composition is proportional to $n_{g,y}$.
- **Negative binomial** (`"nb"`): counts with mean $n_{g,y}\pi_{g,y,l}$ and
  overdispersion $\phi$ (estimated), variance $\mu + \mu^2/\phi$.
- **Dirichlet-multinomial** (`"dm"`): the compositions are drawn from a Dirichlet
  with mean $\pi_{g,y}$ and precision $\alpha_0$; in FLicc $\alpha_0 = n_{g,y}$.
  The variance of the proportions is inflated by
  $(n + \alpha_0)/(1 + \alpha_0) \approx 2$, so a DM fit at sample size $n$ carries
  about the information of a multinomial with $n/2$. Its log-gamma form also
  penalises single-bin misfits less than the multinomial, which makes it more
  robust with messy real data.

`lfdess(lfd, ess.g)` rescales each gear-year to the given effective sample size
(ESS), keeping the proportions; empty gear-years stay empty.

## Why very large sample sizes do harm

Measured fish are not independent: fish from one haul or trip share its length
structure. Raw counts (often thousands) therefore overstate the information by
an order of magnitude. With an overstated sample size:

- the likelihood is dominated by small structural misfits (growth model, binning,
  selectivity shape) rather than the signal, so estimates and their standard
  errors are overconfident;
- log-likelihood differences between alternative assumptions become huge, so
  AIC weights across an ensemble collapse onto a few draws and likelihood profiles
  become jagged or multimodal;
- any discrete effect (a fish entering or leaving the range of the largest growth
  group) is multiplied by $n$.

## Choosing the effective sample size

Empirically, ESS of about 150-200 per gear-year has given the most stable
assessments and ensemble profiles, and 1000 or more behaved poorly in
Monte-Carlo profiling. Practical rules:

- Base ESS on the number of independent sampling units (trips, hauls, vessels)
  where known, e.g. a few fish-equivalents per unit; otherwise start at 150-200 per
  gear-year and test 100 and 300.
- Use the same ESS for gears of similar sampling quality; reduce it for gears
  with few trips.
- Prefer `obs_model = "dm"` with real data; remember it halves the nominal ESS.
- Never fit raw counts of several thousand fish per year without rescaling.

The demonstration below fits the alfonsino data at five effective sample sizes
(`ess_values`), once with the multinomial and once with the Dirichlet-multinomial,
and once more with the raw counts. `lfdess()` rescales the compositions to the
given ESS; `Map()` runs one fit per value. For each fit the table shows the
last-year SPR (`sprcur_flicc()`), its standard error on the log scale (from
`spr_ci_flicc()`) and the largest absolute gradient at the optimum.

```{r ess-demo}
sel_fun <- c("dsnormal", "logistic")
cbg <- c(0.7, 0.3)
stklen <- stocklen(lfd, lhpar, m_model = "constant")

ess_values <- c(50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)

# multinomial: one fit per ESS
fits_mn <- Map(function(ess) {
  fiticc(lfdess(lfd, ess.g = ess), stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "mn"))
}, ess_values)
names(fits_mn) <- paste0("mn_", ess_values)

# Dirichlet-multinomial: one fit per ESS
fits_dm <- Map(function(ess) {
  fiticc(lfdess(lfd, ess.g = ess), stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm"))
}, ess_values)
names(fits_dm) <- paste0("dm_", ess_values)

# raw counts (no rescaling)
fit_raw_mn <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                     settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "mn"))
fit_raw_dm <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                     settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm"))
raw_n <- round(mean(quantSums(lfd[["Trawl"]])))   # fish per year, trawl

fits_mn <- c(fits_mn, raw = list(fit_raw_mn))
fits_dm <- c(fits_dm, raw = list(fit_raw_dm))

# standard error of log SPR in the last year
se_logspr <- function(fit) tail(spr_ci_flicc(fit)$se_log, 1)
ess_table <- data.frame(
  ESS        = c(ess_values, paste0("raw (~", raw_n, ")")),
  SPR_mn     = round(sapply(fits_mn, sprcur_flicc), 3),
  SPR_dm     = round(sapply(fits_dm, sprcur_flicc), 3),
  se_mn      = round(sapply(fits_mn, se_logspr), 3),
  se_dm      = round(sapply(fits_dm, se_logspr), 3),
  maxgrad_dm = signif(sapply(fits_dm, function(fit) fit$max_gradient), 2),
  row.names  = NULL)
ess_table
```

Three things change with the effective sample size:

- **Precision**: the standard error of log SPR shrinks roughly with $1/\sqrt{n}$;
  with large ESS the intervals reflect the sampling of individual fish, not of
  the fishery.
- **Convergence**: the maximum gradient grows at large ESS (here up to
  `r ess_table$maxgrad_dm[5]` at ESS 1000 with `dm`), a sign that the
  likelihood surface becomes sharp and ragged.
- **The estimate itself, for `dm`**: with the multinomial the last-year SPR changes
  little (`r paste(range(ess_table$SPR_mn), collapse = " to ")`),
  but with the Dirichlet-multinomial it ranges from
  `r ess_table$SPR_dm[1]` at ESS 50 to `r ess_table$SPR_dm[5]` at ESS 1000.
  At low ESS the compositions carry little weight against the random walk and
  the catch-share constraint; estimates stabilise from about ESS 150-200 upward.

The alfonsino example has about `r raw_n` fish per gear-year, so its raw counts are
moderate; with the thousands of fish per year common in market sampling the
effects above are much stronger, also for the AIC weights of an ensemble
(section 12).

SPR with 95% intervals for the Dirichlet-multinomial at ESS 50, 200 and 1000 and
for the raw counts:

```{r ess-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot_spr(fits_dm[c("dm_50", "dm_200", "dm_1000", "raw")], ci = TRUE)
```

*Open issue*: estimating the DM precision (overdispersion) instead of fixing
$\alpha_0 = n$ would let the data choose their own weight; this is planned.

# Missing data

FLicc handles missing gear-years directly: a gear-year without samples (all zero
counts) contributes nothing to the composition likelihood, and its F is
informed by the random walk from neighbouring years and by the catch-share
constraint.

```{r missing}
lfd200 <- lfdess(lfd, ess.g = 200)
lfd_miss <- lfd200
lfd_miss[["Gillnet"]][, c("2016", "2017")] <- 0
lfd_miss[["Trawl"]][, "2020"] <- 0
fit200 <- fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                 settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm"))
fit_miss <- fiticc(lfd_miss, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                   settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm"))
flicc_convergence(fit_miss)
```

```{r missing-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot_lfdn(lfd_miss)
plot_spr(list(complete = fit200, gaps = fit_miss), ci = TRUE)
```

Guidelines:

| Situation | Handling |
|---|---|
| a gear missing in some years | keep the zeros; the random walk bridges them (intervals widen) |
| all gears missing in a year | leave the year in (F interpolated) or restrict `years` |
| long gaps or a gear only at the start or end | consider fitting the gear's period separately; selectivity is assumed constant |
| no random walk (`prior_sigmaF = FALSE`) | **avoid with gaps**: F of a gear-year without data is not identified |
| `by_year = TRUE` | fits only years with data; selectivity per year |
| catch by gear missing | use the average split; it only enters through the catch-share constraint |

# Life history and the stock object

```{r stocklen}
stklen
```

`stocklen(lfd, lhpar, m_model)` builds the length-based stock object: weight
$W(L) = aL^b$, maturity as a logistic ogive with `L50` and `L95` (default
`L95 = L50 + 0.2 Linf`), and natural mortality at length:

| `m_model` | $M(L)$ |
|---|---|
| `"constant"` | $M$ |
| `"inverse"` | $M\, L_{ref}/L$ |
| `"Lorenzen"` | Lorenzen weight-based, scaled to $M$ at `reflen` |
| `"Gislason"` | Gislason et al. (2010) from $L$, $L_\infty$, $k$ |

The length model uses $M/k$ (and $Z/k$): what matters is the ratio, so k and M
uncertainty should be considered jointly (as in `mc_flicc()`).

## Check 5: life-history inputs

| | |
|---|---|
| **Look for** | Linf close to the largest regularly observed lengths (Check 3); M/k near the life-history invariant range (often 1-2); L50 below the modal length of the main gear. |
| **Red flags** | Linf well below the largest fish (many fish beyond Linf) or far above it; Linf from another region or sex; M/k outside 0.5-3 without justification. |
| **Action** | Linf is the dominant sensitivity (simulation: a 10% error shifts SPR by +75% / -30%); run Linf sensitivities and include Linf in the ensemble. |

# Selectivity

## Functions and parameterisation

Selectivity is specified per gear in `sel_fun` and estimated on a scale relative
to Linf (log parameters $\theta$), so starting values and priors are
scale-free. With the estimated Linf:

**Logistic** (`"logistic"`):
$$
S(L) = \left[1 + \exp\left(-\ln 19\,\frac{L - L_{50}}{L_{95} - L_{50}}\right)\right]^{-1},
\quad L_{50} = e^{\theta_1} L_\infty,\; L_{95} - L_{50} = e^{\theta_2} L_\infty .
$$

**Double-sided normal** (`"dsnormal"`, dome):
$$
S(L) = \exp\left[-\frac{(L - L_{mode})^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],\quad
\sigma = \begin{cases}\sigma_L & L < L_{mode}\\ \sigma_R & L \ge L_{mode}\end{cases},
\quad L_{mode} = e^{\theta_1}L_\infty,\; \sigma_L = e^{\theta_2}L_\infty,\; \sigma_R = e^{\theta_3}L_\infty .
$$

**Normal** (`"normal"`): as above with $\sigma_L = \sigma_R$.

Starting values: the mode (or L50) at the gear's observed modal length, spreads
of 0.1 Linf. Selectivity is evaluated at bin mid-points and is constant over
time.

```{r sel}
plot_sel(fit200)
selpars_flicc(fit200)
```

## Fixing selectivity parameters

`sel_fixed` fixes parameters on the length scale by gear, e.g. from mesh
experiments:

```{r sel-fixed, eval = FALSE}
fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
       settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm"),
       sel_fixed = list(Gillnet = list(SL50 = 30, SL95 = 34)))   # logistic
# dsnormal: list(mode = 24, lsd = 3, rsd = 1000)  (rsd = 1000: flat right limb)
# normal:   list(mode = 24, sd = 4)
```

## Exploring selectivity shapes

`plot_selfun()` draws a selectivity function for a range of parameter values,
over the observed composition of a gear and with reference lengths. It helps to
choose values for `sel_fixed` and the dome scenarios below:

```{r selfun, fig.height = 4.5}
gn <- lfd[["Gillnet"]]
Lmid_g <- as.numeric(dimnames(gn)$len) + 0.5
Lmean_g <- round(sum(Lmid_g * apply(gn@.Data, 1, sum)) / sum(gn@.Data), 1)
ref_L <- c(L50mat = 31.2, Lmean = Lmean_g, Linf = 55.7)
plot_selfun("dsnormal", list(mode = 34, lsd = 4, rsd = c(1000, 33, 22, 14)), lfd = gn, ref = ref_L)
plot_selfun("logistic", list(SL50 = c(28, 31, 34), SL95 = 37), lfd = gn, ref = ref_L)
```

A double-sided normal with a very large right-hand SD (`rsd = 1000`) has a flat
right limb, i.e. no dome; smaller values give mild (about 0.6 Linf), moderate
(0.4 Linf) and strong (0.25 Linf) doming. `sel_curve_flicc()` returns the
values of a curve.

## Dome sensitivity: a recommended standard run

Slight doming (large fish less selected or less available) is hard to detect
from length data, and an unmodelled dome is read as higher F. A sensitivity over
fixed dome shapes is therefore recommended for every gear assumed logistic.
`dome_sens_flicc()` refits the model with that gear as a double-sided normal
whose right-hand SD is fixed at a sequence of values (default
`c(1000, 0.6, 0.4, 0.25) x Linf`); the mode and left-hand SD are estimated, all
other settings and data as in the base fit.

```{r dome-sens, fig.height = 4.5}
ds <- dome_sens_flicc(fit200, gear = "Gillnet")
ds$table
plot_dome_sens(ds)
plot_dome_sens(ds, "spr", ci = TRUE)
```

The run with `rsd = 1000` reproduces the logistic base fit (SPR
`r ds$table$SPR_last[2]` vs `r ds$table$SPR_last[1]`), which is the check that the
scenarios are comparable. For the gillnet, no, mild and moderate domes fit
equally well (dAIC `r paste(ds$table$dAIC[2:4], collapse = ", ")`), while the
strong dome is worse (dAIC `r ds$table$dAIC[5]`). The data therefore cannot tell
whether large fish are fully selected or mildly less so, and over that range the
last-year SPR goes from `r ds$table$SPR_last[2]` to `r ds$table$SPR_last[4]`.
Read the table as a sensitivity, not a model selection: report the range of
status across the domes the data cannot reject. With a tail cut the scenarios
differ less, because the bins where the dome acts are excluded:

```{r dome-sens-cut}
fit200_cut <- fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                     settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", tail_cut = 47))
ds_cut <- dome_sens_flicc(fit200_cut, gear = "Gillnet", se = FALSE)
data.frame(scenario = ds$table$scenario, SPR_no_cut = ds$table$SPR_last,
           SPR_cut47 = ds_cut$table$SPR_last)
```

Here the cut narrows the range across no to moderate doming from
`r ds$table$SPR_last[2]`-`r ds$table$SPR_last[4]` to
`r ds_cut$table$SPR_last[2]`-`r ds_cut$table$SPR_last[4]`.

The sensitivity is meant for gears assumed asymptotic. For a gear already fitted
as a dome (here the trawl, estimated right-hand SD about
`r round(exp(fit200$par$mpd[fit200$par$par == "Sm"][3]) * 55.7, 1)` cm), fixing a
wide right-hand SD forces a shape the data reject, which shows as very large dAIC.

## Choosing selectivity

- Use logistic unless gear knowledge (gillnet mesh, hook size, availability of
  large fish) supports a dome.
- A dome fitted without support absorbs a shortage of large fish that may come
  from F; SPR then becomes optimistic.
- Several gears sampling different length ranges make domes more identifiable.
- A tail cut (section 11) reduces the cost of an unmodelled mild dome
  (*simulation*: a strong dome fitted as logistic, -17% bias in SPR; with a cut at
  0.8 Linf, +1%).
- Always run the dome sensitivity for gears assumed logistic, and report it.

## Check 6: selectivity plausibility

| | |
|---|---|
| **Look for** | Ascending limbs consistent with the gear and the left limb of the compositions; domes only where expected. |
| **Red flags** | Very narrow domes; $\sigma_R$ at very small values for a gear expected to be logistic; L50 below the smallest sampled fish. |
| **Action** | Compare logistic and dome by AIC and by status; fix parameters from external information; use a tail cut. |

# Model

## Fishing mortality and total mortality

$F_{g,y}(L) = F_{g,y} S_g(L)$, $Z_y(L) = M(L) + \sum_g F_{g,y}(L)$. Gear shares of F
are informed by `catch_by_gear` through a soft constraint on the predicted
catch shares (`catch.sd`, default 0.05).

## Population model

`pop_model = "gtg"` (default, LBSPR): growth-type groups
$L_{\infty,h} = L_\infty(1 + \mathrm{CVL}\, z_h)$, $z_h$ on
`seq(-maxsd, maxsd, length = ngtg)` (13 groups, `maxsd = 2`), weights
$\propto \phi(z_h)$, and survival across bin $i$:
$$
N_{i+1,h} = N_{i,h}\left(\frac{L_{\infty,h} - L_{i+1}}{L_{\infty,h} - L_i}\right)^{Z_i/k}.
$$
`pop_model = "gamma"` follows fishblicc (gamma-distributed Linf, numerical
integration; slower). Both are equilibrium models: each year is explained by
the equilibrium at that year's F (section 10.2 on the consequences).

## Status: SPR

$$
\mathrm{SPR}_y = \frac{\sum_L N_{F_y}(L) W(L) P_{mat}(L)}{\sum_L N_0(L) W(L) P_{mat}(L)} .
$$

# Fitting and fit checks

```{r fit}
t0 <- system.time(
  fit <- fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm"))
)
t0[["elapsed"]]
sigmaF_flicc(fit)
```

From here on, `fit` is the reference fit (Dirichlet-multinomial, ESS 200).

## Settings

| Setting | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `pop_model` | `"gtg"` | `"gtg"`, `"gamma"` (`"gtg.dyn"`: development) |
| `obs_model` | `"mn"` | `"mn"`, `"nb"`, `"dm"` |
| `CVL` | 0.1 | CV of Linf among growth groups (fixed unless `CVL.sd`) |
| `ngtg`, `maxsd` | 13, 2 | GTG grid (as LBSPR) |
| `Mpow` | 0 | M/k at length $\propto (L_\infty/L)^{Mpow}$ |
| `linf.sd`, `Mk.sd`, `CVL.sd` | `NULL` | estimate with a prior around the input |
| `sigmaF` | 0.3 | random-walk SD of log F, fixed |
| `prior_sigmaF` | – | `c(mean, sd, use)`: estimate sigmaF with a prior; `FALSE`: no random walk |
| `F_re` | `FALSE` | log F as random effects (Laplace), sigmaF estimated |
| `catch.sd` | 0.05 | SD of the catch-share constraint |
| `tail_cut` | `NULL` | exclude bins with lower bound `>= tail_cut` (length) |
| `Lplus` | `NULL` | pool bins with lower bound `>= Lplus` |
| `rob_eps` | 0 | robust likelihood: $(1 - \epsilon)\pi + \epsilon/n_{bins}$ |
| `spr_ref` | 40 | SPR target(s) (%) whose Fspr is stored with the fit |
| `FM_min`, `FM_max` | 0.05, 4 | bounds on apical F/M (soft penalty) |
| `tail_warning` | `FALSE` | warn about fish beyond the largest GTG Linf |

Further arguments of `fiticc()`: `n_restart` (restarts while the gradient is
large), `se = FALSE` (skip standard errors), `start` (e.g. `fit$opt$par`),
`years`, `by_year`, `sel_fixed`.

## Check 7: convergence

```{r check-conv}
flicc_convergence(fit)
```

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pass** | convergence code 0, maximum gradient < 0.001-0.01, positive-definite Hessian, finite standard errors. |
| **Red flags** | large gradient after restarts; non-positive-definite Hessian; parameters at bounds (F/M at `FM_min`/`FM_max`, very small selectivity spreads). |
| **Action** | more restarts (`n_restart`); restart from `fit$opt$par`; simplify selectivity (logistic, fewer gears); check sample sizes; a tail cut or `rob_eps` if the tail drives the problem. |

## Check 8: fit to the compositions

```{r check-len, fig.height = 6}
plot_len(fit, by_gear = TRUE, year = 2021:2024)
plot_len(fit)
```

| | |
|---|---|
| **Look for** | Predictions through the observed modes and descending limbs in every gear. |
| **Red flags** | Systematic misfit of the left limb (selectivity), of the tail (Linf, CVL, dome), or of one gear only; the misfit changing sign between periods (time-varying selectivity or sampling). |
| **Action** | Revisit selectivity form and Linf; tail cut; split periods. |

## Check 9: retrospective consistency

The model is refitted with the last one, two and three years removed (`peels`);
`Map()` runs one fit per peel. Mohn's rho compares the terminal SPR of each peel
with the SPR of the same year in the full fit.

```{r check-retro, fig.height = 4}
yrs <- as.numeric(dimnames(lfd200[[1]])$year)
peels <- 1:3

retro <- Map(function(p) {
  fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm"),
         years = head(yrs, -p), se = FALSE)
}, peels)
names(retro) <- paste0("peel", peels)
plot_spr(c(list(full = fit), retro))

spr_full <- c(fit$report$spr)
spr_peel <- sapply(retro, sprcur_flicc)               # terminal SPR of each peel
spr_same <- spr_full[length(spr_full) - peels]        # same years in the full fit
mohn_rho <- mean((spr_peel - spr_same) / spr_same)
round(mohn_rho, 3)
```

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pass** | Mohn's rho for SPR within about ±0.2. |
| **Red flags** | Consistent revisions in one direction (the terminal SPR is systematically revised up or down). |
| **Action** | Check for trends in selectivity or sampling; in a rebuild, an equilibrium model is expected to under-estimate SPR at the end of the series (section 10.2). |

# Fishing mortality over time

Log F by gear follows a random walk,
$$
\log F_{g,y} = \log F_{g,y-1} + \varepsilon_{g,y}, \qquad \varepsilon_{g,y} \sim N(0, \sigma_F^2).
$$
It links the years, so selectivity and F are estimated jointly from all
compositions, and it bridges years without data. The options differ in how
$\sigma_F$ is treated.

The four options for $\sigma_F$ are fitted below to the same data (ESS 200,
Dirichlet-multinomial). Only the F settings differ, so each option has its own
`settings` list; `Map()` fits them in turn.

```{r f-options}
f_settings <- list(
  fixed_0.3 = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", sigmaF = 0.3),                       # default
  prior     = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", prior_sigmaF = c(log(0.5), 0.3, 1)), # penalised
  F_re      = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", F_re = TRUE),                        # random effects
  no_RW     = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", prior_sigmaF = FALSE))               # no random walk

fits_F <- Map(function(set) {
  fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg, settings = set)
}, f_settings)

data.frame(option   = names(fits_F),
           sigmaF   = round(sapply(fits_F, sigmaF_flicc), 3),
           SPR_last = round(sapply(fits_F, sprcur_flicc), 3),
           se_log   = round(sapply(fits_F, se_logspr), 3),
           row.names = NULL)
```

`sigmaF_flicc()` returns the fixed or estimated $\sigma_F$ (NA without a random
walk). The SPR trajectories with 95% intervals, and the apical F by year
(`report$Fap`):

```{r f-options-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot_spr(fits_F, ci = TRUE)

F_by_option <- FLQuants(fixed_0.3 = fits_F$fixed_0.3$report$Fap,
                        prior     = fits_F$prior$report$Fap,
                        F_re      = fits_F$F_re$report$Fap,
                        no_RW     = fits_F$no_RW$report$Fap)
ggplot(F_by_option, aes(year, data, colour = qname)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Apical F", colour = NULL) + theme_bw()
```

The estimated $\sigma_F$ of the penalised and random-effects options is much
smaller than 0.3, so their F trajectories are smoother; without a random walk F
follows each year's composition. To see what $\sigma_F$ does, the next runs fix it
at a range of values (`sigmaF_values`):

```{r sigmaF-range, fig.height = 4}
sigmaF_values <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.6, 1)

fits_sigmaF <- Map(function(sF) {
  fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", sigmaF = sF), se = FALSE)
}, sigmaF_values)
names(fits_sigmaF) <- paste0("sigmaF_", sigmaF_values)

plot_spr(fits_sigmaF)
data.frame(sigmaF   = sigmaF_values,
           SPR_last = round(sapply(fits_sigmaF, sprcur_flicc), 3),
           neg_logL = round(sapply(fits_sigmaF, function(fit) fit$opt$objective), 1))
```

Small values force F (and SPR) towards a flat line; from about 0.3 upward the
trajectories change little. The objective (`neg_logL`) includes the random-walk
penalty, which is why it cannot be used to choose $\sigma_F$ directly: it always
favours the smallest value that the compositions tolerate.

## Default: sigmaF fixed

`sigmaF = 0.3` (the default) fixes the year-to-year standard deviation of log F,
roughly a 30% typical annual change. It is fast, cannot collapse, and the
simulations showed that it removes most of the smoothing lag (next section).
Change it where fleet dynamics are known to be smoother (0.2) or more variable
(0.5).

## Estimating sigmaF with a prior (penalised)

With `prior_sigmaF = c(mu, sd, 1)`, $\sigma_F$ is a fixed-effect parameter and the
objective is
$$
-\log L = -\log L_{data} - \sum_{g,y} \log \phi\left(\log F_{g,y} - \log F_{g,y-1};\, 0, \sigma_F\right)
          - \log \phi\left(\log \sigma_F;\, \mu, sd\right).
$$
Each random-walk term contributes $-\log \sigma_F$, so the joint maximum favours
small $\sigma_F$ with flat F whenever the data do not resist: the estimate is
pulled down (here `r round(sigmaF_flicc(fits_F$prior), 3)`), and only the prior keeps it
away from 0. Without a prior (`prior_sigmaF = c(NA, NA, 1)`) it collapses; FLicc
warns.

## F as random effects (`F_re = TRUE`)

The log F are integrated out,
$$
L(\theta) = \int L_{data}(\theta, \mathbf F)\, p(\mathbf F \mid \sigma_F)\, d\mathbf F,
$$
by the Laplace approximation (TMB): for each value of the other parameters
$\theta$ (selectivity, $\sigma_F$), the F path is optimised and the curvature
around it enters the marginal likelihood. Consequences:

- $\sigma_F$ is estimated from the marginal likelihood, which properly accounts for
  the uncertainty of the F path (here `r round(sigmaF_flicc(fits_F$F_re), 3)`). It can still
  go to small values when the compositions carry little year-to-year
  information; a weak prior `c(log(0.3), 0.5, 1)` is used unless another is given.
- Standard errors (e.g. of log SPR) include the uncertainty of the F process.
- Fitting is slower:

```{r f-re-time}
system.time(fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg, settings = f_settings$fixed_0.3))
system.time(fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg, settings = f_settings$F_re))
```

Use it for a final assessment and to estimate $\sigma_F$ once; then fix it for
repeated fits: `sigmaF = sigmaF_flicc(fit_re)`. `F_re = TRUE` with `sigmaF` given
keeps the random effects but fixes $\sigma_F$.

## No random walk and separate years

`prior_sigmaF = FALSE` estimates each year's F freely with shared selectivity
(LBSPR fitted year by year, with common selectivity): no smoothing lag, but noisier
F and no information for years without data. `by_year = TRUE` fits each year
completely separately (including selectivity).

| Option | Settings | sigmaF | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| fixed (default) | `sigmaF = 0.3` | fixed | routine, MSE, ensembles |
| penalised with prior | `prior_sigmaF = c(log(0.5), 0.3, 1)` | estimated, pulled down | comparison with earlier versions |
| random effects | `F_re = TRUE` | marginal likelihood | final assessment; estimate sigmaF once |
| no random walk | `prior_sigmaF = FALSE` | – | complete data, maximum responsiveness |
| separate years | `by_year = TRUE` | – | checks of selectivity change |

## Lag under changing F

An equilibrium model explains each year's composition by the equilibrium at that
year's F. After a change in F, the large fish adjust only over many years, so the
estimated SPR lags behind (*simulation*, rebuild from 3x to 0.7x Fmsy):

| F model | SPR trend recovered, no cut | with cut at 0.8 Linf |
|---|---|---|
| sigmaF estimated (collapsing) | 14% | 26% |
| sigmaF fixed 0.3 | 27% | 50% |
| sigmaF fixed 1 | 29% | 57% |
| no random walk | 30% | 59% |

The smoothing lag of the random walk is largely removed at sigmaF = 0.3; larger
values add little responsiveness but more year-to-year noise (+10 to +50%). The
rest of the lag comes from the data (the tail carries the memory of past F) and
from recruitment rising during recovery under a stock-recruitment relationship.
In a rebuild from deep depletion the equilibrium model stays pessimistic.

# Growth variability and life-history priors

## CVL

`CVL` is the coefficient of variation of Linf among growth-type groups. It sets how
far individual growth spreads the length composition, mostly in the tail: the
fastest-growing groups determine how many fish occur near and beyond Linf. It is
fixed at its input value unless `CVL.sd` is given; typical values are 0.07-0.15.

The sensitivity below refits the model for three CVL values (`cvl_values`),
without and with a tail cut at 47 cm; `Map()` runs one fit per value.

```{r cvl-sens, fig.height = 4}
cvl_values <- c(0.07, 0.10, 0.13)

fits_cvl <- Map(function(cvl) {
  fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = cvl, obs_model = "dm"), se = FALSE)
}, cvl_values)
names(fits_cvl) <- paste0("CVL_", cvl_values)

fits_cvl_cut <- Map(function(cvl) {
  fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = cvl, obs_model = "dm", tail_cut = 47), se = FALSE)
}, cvl_values)
names(fits_cvl_cut) <- paste0("CVL_", cvl_values, "_cut47")

cvl_table <- data.frame(CVL       = cvl_values,
                        SPR_no_cut = round(sapply(fits_cvl, sprcur_flicc), 3),
                        SPR_cut47  = round(sapply(fits_cvl_cut, sprcur_flicc), 3),
                        row.names = NULL)
cvl_table
plot_spr(c(fits_cvl, fits_cvl_cut))
```

Status is sensitive to CVL because CVL shapes the tail: here SPR ranges
`r min(cvl_table$SPR_no_cut)`-`r max(cvl_table$SPR_no_cut)` over CVL 0.07-0.13
without a cut and `r min(cvl_table$SPR_cut47)`-`r max(cvl_table$SPR_cut47)` with a
cut at 47 cm.

## maxsd and ngtg

The growth groups are placed at $z_h$ on `seq(-maxsd, maxsd, length = ngtg)` with
normal weights. Truncating the normal at `maxsd` reduces the realised CV of the
groups below CVL and caps the largest group at $L_\infty(1 + \text{maxsd}\cdot\text{CVL})$:

The realised spread can be computed directly from the group positions `z` and
their normal weights `w`; the factor multiplies CVL:

```{r maxsd-cv}
z <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 13)          # maxsd = 2, ngtg = 13 (default)
w <- dnorm(z) / sum(dnorm(z))
sqrt(sum(w * z^2))                        # realised CV factor

z <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 19)          # maxsd = 3, ngtg = 19
w <- dnorm(z) / sum(dnorm(z))
sqrt(sum(w * z^2))

55.7 * (1 + c(2, 3) * 0.1)                # largest group Linf for maxsd 2 and 3
```

With the LBSPR default (`maxsd = 2`, 13 groups) the realised CV is about 0.9 x
CVL; `maxsd = 3` gives almost exactly CVL and allows larger fish. The number of
groups matters little beyond about 13.

The fits below compare the two settings (`maxsd_values` with matching
`ngtg_values`), without and with the tail cut; `Map()` takes the two vectors in
parallel.

```{r maxsd-sens}
maxsd_values <- c(2, 3)
ngtg_values  <- c(13, 19)

fits_maxsd <- Map(function(maxsd, ngtg) {
  fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", maxsd = maxsd, ngtg = ngtg), se = FALSE)
}, maxsd_values, ngtg_values)

fits_maxsd_cut <- Map(function(maxsd, ngtg) {
  fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", maxsd = maxsd, ngtg = ngtg,
                         tail_cut = 47), se = FALSE)
}, maxsd_values, ngtg_values)

data.frame(maxsd      = maxsd_values,
           ngtg       = ngtg_values,
           SPR_no_cut = round(sapply(fits_maxsd, sprcur_flicc), 3),
           SPR_cut47  = round(sapply(fits_maxsd_cut, sprcur_flicc), 3))
```

Recommendation: keep the LBSPR default for comparability and treat `maxsd = 3`
as a sensitivity; with a tail cut the choice matters little, because the
affected bins lie far above the cut. The effective CV matters when CVL is taken
from external growth studies: with `maxsd = 2`, a CVL input of 0.1 corresponds
to a realised spread of about 0.09.

## Estimating Linf, M/k and CVL with priors

By default growth and natural mortality are fixed. `linf.sd`, `Mk.sd` and
`CVL.sd` estimate them with normal priors on the log scale around the inputs:
$$
\log L_\infty \sim N(\log L_\infty^{in}, \texttt{linf.sd}^2), \quad
\log (M/k) \sim N(\log (M/k)^{in}, \texttt{Mk.sd}^2), \quad
\log \mathrm{CVL} \sim N(\log \mathrm{CVL}^{in}, \texttt{CVL.sd}^2),
$$
so each sd is approximately a CV (e.g. `linf.sd = 0.05`: about ±10% at 95%).

The fit below estimates all three with priors. The estimates are on the log
scale: $L_\infty$ = `exp(log_Linf)`, $M/k$ = `exp(log_Mk)` and CVL =
`1 / sqrt(exp(log_Galpha))`; the column `se` is approximately the posterior CV
(for `log_Galpha` divide by 2).

```{r priors, fig.height = 4}
fit_pri <- fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                  settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm",
                                  linf.sd = 0.05, Mk.sd = 0.1, CVL.sd = 0.25))

est <- fit_pri$par[fit_pri$par$par %in% c("log_Linf", "log_Mk", "log_Galpha"), ]
est
exp(est$mpd[est$par == "log_Linf"])            # Linf (input 55.7)
exp(est$mpd[est$par == "log_Mk"])              # M/k  (input 0.162 / 0.08 = 2.03)
1 / sqrt(exp(est$mpd[est$par == "log_Galpha"])) # CVL  (input 0.1)

plot_spr(list(fixed = fit, priors = fit_pri), ci = TRUE)
```

```{r priors-numbers, include = FALSE}
pp <- function(nm, col = "mpd") est[[col]][est$par == nm][1]
```

Here the length data pull Linf up to about `r round(exp(pp("log_Linf")), 1)`
(posterior CV `r round(pp("log_Linf", "se"), 3)` against a prior CV of 0.05), and
because a larger Linf means the fish in the catch are relatively younger, SPR
drops markedly. The posterior CVs of M/k and CVL stay close to their prior CVs:
the data say little about them. A shift of this size in Linf is a finding to
check against growth studies, not a result to accept; run the assessment with
Linf fixed at the alternative values as a sensitivity.

Notes:

- **k** is not estimated separately: the length model depends on M/k (and Z/k), so
  uncertainty in k and M is expressed through `Mk.sd`. k still sets the time scale
  of the annual F estimates (F is estimated as F/k).
- Length data carry limited information on Linf and CVL, and both are confounded
  with dome-shaped selectivity and the tail; a posterior CV close to the prior CV
  means the data are uninformative. Large moves away from the input (several prior
  SDs) indicate a conflict between the data and the life history, to be
  investigated rather than accepted.
- For ensembles, drawing the life-history parameters and keeping them fixed in
  each fit (`mc_flicc()`) is usually better behaved than estimating them.

# Tail of the length composition

## Tail cut

`tail_cut = L` excludes bins with lower bound $\geq L$ from the likelihood;
observed and predicted compositions are truncated and the predictions
renormalised,
$$
\pi_{l \mid L < L_{cut}} = \pi_l \Big/ \sum_{l' : L_{l'} < L_{cut}} \pi_{l'} .
$$
This is exact conditioning: the model still describes the whole population with
its input CVL, SPR and reference points use all lengths, and CVL needs no
adjustment. `tail_cut` is an **absolute length** (as `Lplus`), so all sensitivity
runs and ensemble draws use the same bins. (Values <= 1.5 are read as a fraction
of Linf, with a warning.)

```{r tailcut, fig.height = 4}
fit_cut <- fiticc(lfd200, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                  settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", tail_cut = 47))  # ~0.85 x Linf
fit_cut$tmb_data$LLB[fit_cut$tmb_data$cut_bin + 1]
plot_spr(list(no_cut = fit, cut_47 = fit_cut), ci = TRUE)
```

*Simulation* (stable F, correct Linf unless stated):

| | no cut | cut at 0.80-0.85 x Linf |
|---|---|---|
| CVL input 0.07 / 0.10 / 0.13 (true 0.1) | +9 / -1 / -11% | +13 / +9 / +4% |
| strong dome on one gear fitted as logistic | -17% | +1% |
| SPR trend recovered in a rebuild (sigmaF 0.3) | 27% | ~50% |
| Linf input 0.9 / 1.1 x true | +91 / -40% | +74 / -28% |

The cut halves the CVL sensitivity, removes the bias of a strong unmodelled dome
and roughly doubles responsiveness; it costs a small positive bias (+7 to +10%)
and more noise under stable F, and does not remove the Linf sensitivity.
Starting value: 0.80-0.85 x Linf, fixed across fits.

## Plus group, robust likelihood, GTG range

- `Lplus = L` pools bins with lower bound $\geq L$ into one (the total counts, the
  shape does not).
- `rob_eps = 0.001` bounds the cost of a few fish in bins the model barely reaches.
- The largest growth group stops at $L_\infty(1 + \text{maxsd}\cdot\text{CVL})$; with
  `maxsd = 2` the effective CV is about 0.9 x CVL. Fish beyond it get near-zero
  probability; a tail cut makes this irrelevant.

# Reference points and status

## Fspr

The fit stores Fspr for `settings$spr_ref` (default 40%), computed in TMB:

```{r refpts}
fspr_flicc(fit)                 # stored Fspr40
fspr_flicc(fit, spr = 30)       # computed
fcur_flicc(fit); sprcur_flicc(fit)
```

## From SPR to relative spawning biomass

With Beverton-Holt recruitment of steepness $s$,
$$
\frac{B}{B_0} = \frac{4s\,\mathrm{SPR} - (1 - s)}{5s - 1}, \qquad
\frac{B}{B_{tgt}} = \frac{4s\,\mathrm{SPR} - (1-s)}{4s\,\mathrm{SPR}_{tgt} - (1-s)} ,
$$
so SPR overstates depletion when $s < 1$. `spr2brel()` and
`flicc2FLStockR(s = )` apply the mapping (F is unchanged):

```{r steepness, fig.height = 5}
round(spr2brel(c(0.2, 0.3, 0.4), s = 0.75, sprref = 40), 3)
plot_LBAdvice(FLStocks(SPR = flicc2FLStockR(fit, rel = TRUE),
                       relB_s0.75 = flicc2FLStockR(fit, rel = TRUE, s = 0.75)), panel = 1)
```

`eqstklen(fit, s = )` gives the equilibrium curves and MSY proxies.

## Status over selectivity and F: contour plots

`contour_flicc()` computes, for each gear, yield per recruit and SPR over a grid
of the gear's F and its selectivity location, with the other gears held at their
current state. The location is `SL50` for a logistic gear and the mode for a
dome; the curve is shifted along the length axis with its shape kept.
`plot_contour_flicc()` draws the result with one row per gear: yield on the
left, spawning potential on the right, both in % on the same colour scale
(dark blue = 100%, red = 0%):

- **YPR%**: yield per recruit as a percentage of its maximum over the grid;
- **SPR%**: spawning potential ratio in %.

The black lines are SPR 40% (solid) and 20% (dashed), the point is the current
state with dotted guides to the axes, and the dotted horizontal line is the
length at 50% maturity (Lmat).

```{r contour, fig.height = 8.5, fig.width = 9}
cf <- contour_flicc(fit)
cf$current
plot_contour_flicc(cf)
```

Per-recruit results assume constant recruitment. With a steepness `s`, the same
surfaces are converted under a Beverton-Holt relationship to **SSB%**
(spawning biomass in % of unfished, $B/B_0$) and **Yield%** (equilibrium yield
in % of its maximum over the grid), with
$R/R_0 = \frac{4s\,SPR - (1-s)}{(5s-1)\,SPR}$ and
$B/B_0 = \frac{4s\,SPR - (1-s)}{5s-1}$. The black lines are then SSB 40% and 20%:

```{r contour-s, fig.height = 8.5, fig.width = 9}
plot_contour_flicc(cf, s = 0.75)
```

```{r selF-numbers, include = FALSE}
gn_cur <- cf$current[cf$current$gear == "Gillnet", ]
gn_s <- cf$surface[cf$surface$gear == "Gillnet", ]
eng <- FLicc:::pr_engine_flicc(fit); st <- FLicc:::gear_state_flicc(fit)
pr_gn <- function(loc, Fg) {
  S <- function(g, p) sel_curve_flicc(st$Lmid, st$type[[g]], p)
  eng(st$F[["Trawl"]] * S("Trawl", st$pars[["Trawl"]]) +
      Fg * S("Gillnet", FLicc:::shift_sel_flicc(st$type[["Gillnet"]], st$pars[["Gillnet"]], loc)))
}
ymax <- max(gn_s$YPR)
v <- pr_gn(cf$Lmat, gn_cur$F)
gn_lmat <- list(SPR = v[["SPR"]], YPRrel = v[["YPR"]] / ymax)
f40 <- tryCatch(uniroot(function(f) pr_gn(gn_cur$loc, f)[["SPR"]] - 0.4, c(0, gn_cur$F))$root,
                error = function(e) NA)
gn_cut <- if (is.na(f40)) "more than 100" else round(100 * (1 - f40 / gn_cur$F))
```

How to read it:

- Moving left from the point (less F) or up (larger fish first caught) raises
  SPR; the YPR isopleths show what that costs, or gains, in yield per recruit.
- Here the gillnet catches at `SL50` = `r round(gn_cur$loc, 1)`, below Lmat
  (`r round(cf$Lmat, 1)`). At its current F, raising `SL50` to Lmat gives an SPR
  of about `r round(100 * gn_lmat$SPR)`% and `r round(100 * gn_lmat$YPRrel)`% of
  the maximum YPR (now `r round(100 * gn_cur$YPRrel)`%); reaching SPR 40% at the
  current `SL50` instead needs the gillnet F cut by about `r gn_cut`%.
- Without `s` the surfaces are per-recruit results; with `s` they include the
  loss of recruitment at low spawning biomass, so yield falls off more steeply
  at high F. Both are equilibrium results at the fitted life history, a guide to
  direction and scale, not a forecast.

`gear =` selects gears (rows), `n` the grid resolution, `Fmax` and `Lrange` the
axes, `ref` the black reference levels and `levels` the grey isopleths.

# Length-based indicators

## LBIspr

For each gear, `LBIspr()` compares the observed proportion of large fish with
the proportion expected at the reference $F_{\mathrm{SPR}x}$:

1. Equilibrium numbers-at-length at $F_{\mathrm{SPR}x}$, $N^{ref}(L)$, and the
   reference catch composition of gear $g$, $v_g(L) = N^{ref}(L) S_g(L)$ (retained
   bins only, i.e. below the tail cut).
2. Threshold length $L^*_g$: the length at which the cumulative $v_g$ reaches the
   fraction `thresh` (default 0.75) of its total.
3. Reference proportion above the threshold,
   $P^{ref}_g = \sum_{L \ge L^*_g} v_g(L) / \sum_L v_g(L)$ (about $1 -$ `thresh`).
4. Observed proportion in year $y$,
   $P^{obs}_{g,y} = \sum_{L \ge L^*_g} y_{g,y,L} / \sum_L y_{g,y,L}$.
5. Indicator $\mathrm{LBI}_{g,y} = P^{obs}_{g,y}/P^{ref}_g$.

$\mathrm{LBI} = 1$: as many large fish as at the target; $< 1$: fewer, i.e. F above
$F_{\mathrm{SPR}x}$. The threshold lengths are returned as `attr(, "Lref")`.

```{r lbispr}
lbi <- LBIspr(fit, spr = 40, thresh = 0.75)
attr(lbi, "Lref")
plot_LBIspr(fit, thresh = 0.75)
plot_LBIp(fit, year = 2024)
```

## LBImean

`LBImean()` is the model-based analogue of the ICES mean-length indicator
$\bar L/L_{F=M}$: the reference mean length (above `lc`, default the gear's
50% selectivity length) is computed from the fitted model at $F = M$
(`ref = "FM"`) or at $F_{\mathrm{SPR}x}$ (`ref = "spr"`), using the fitted growth
variability and gear selectivity, including domes.

```{r lbimean}
LBImean(fit, ref = "FM")
```

## Indicators and the tail cut

Both indicators use the fit's tail cut by default (`tail_cut = NULL`), so the
indicator and the likelihood use the same bins; `tail_cut = FALSE` uses all bins.

## Check 10: indicators against status

| | |
|---|---|
| **Look for** | LBIspr and SPR/SPR40 telling the same story; similar indicators across gears. |
| **Red flags** | Gears disagreeing strongly (selectivity misfit or sampling); indicator noise much larger than the SPR trend. |
| **Action** | Use the more informative gear; pool gears (`pool` in `flicc.sa()`); smooth in the harvest control rule. |

# Monte-Carlo ensembles

`mc_flicc()` propagates uncertainty in the life-history inputs. It draws Linf,
k, M and L50 (correlated, from FishLife) and CVL, refits the model for each draw
and keeps each fit's SPR, F, selectivity and log-likelihood. Within each refit
the drawn values are fixed; they are not estimated. The coefficients of
variation of the draws are set with `cv`; the default is
`cv = list(linf = 0.10, k = 0.1, M = 0.15, L50 = 0.10, CVL = 0.1)`.

**Drawing CVL or not.** CVL shapes the tail of the predicted composition. When
it varies between draws together with Linf, the largest growth group moves
across bin boundaries, and fish in those bins switch between near-zero and
positive probability. This produces jumps in the log-likelihood between draws
and can make the profile over draws look bimodal. Setting `CVL = 0` in `cv`
keeps CVL at its input value in every draw, so the ensemble reflects Linf, k, M
and L50 only; CVL can then be examined as a separate sensitivity (section 11).
The tail cut has a similar effect, because it removes the bins concerned; as a
length, it is the same for every draw.

The example runs two ensembles of 30 draws on the fit with the tail cut
(ESS 200): one with CVL drawn (the default) and one with CVL fixed. The same
`seed` gives the same Linf, k, M and L50 draws in both.

```{r mc}
mc_cvl_drawn <- mc_flicc(fit_cut, nsim = 30, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)

mc_cvl_fixed <- mc_flicc(fit_cut, nsim = 30, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE,
                         cv = list(linf = 0.10, k = 0.1, M = 0.15, L50 = 0.10, CVL = 0))
```

`mc_spr_tab()` summarises the SPR by year over the draws: the base fit (`mle`),
the unweighted mean (`mean_uw`), the AIC-weighted mean (`mean_w`), the number of
draws within 20 AIC units of the best (`n_retained`) and the effective number of
draws after weighting (`n_eff`). The last year:

```{r mc-tab}
tab_drawn <- mc_spr_tab(mc_cvl_drawn)
tab_fixed <- mc_spr_tab(mc_cvl_fixed)
rbind(CVL_drawn = tail(tab_drawn, 1),
      CVL_fixed = tail(tab_fixed, 1))
```

The profile plots show SPR against the log-likelihood of each draw:

```{r mc-plots, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_mcprofile(mc_cvl_drawn)
plot_mcprofile(mc_cvl_fixed)
plot_mcsprdist(mc_cvl_fixed)
```

Recommendations:

- Rescale the sample size first (ESS about 150-200). With large sample sizes the
  log-likelihood differences between draws grow, and the AIC weights concentrate
  on few draws.
- Use the tail cut and fixed sigmaF in the base fit; every draw inherits its
  settings.
- Report the unweighted ensemble (`mean_uw`) alongside the weighted one; AIC
  weighting across life-history draws mixes data fit with prior uncertainty and
  should be treated with caution.

# Use in an MSE

`flicc.sa()` wraps `fiticc()` as the estimation step of an `mse` management
procedure, with `lbi.hcr()`, `rfb.flicc.hcr()` and `flicc.is()` for the
harvest control rule and implementation:

```{r mse, eval = FALSE}
est <- mseCtrl(method = flicc.sa, args = list(
  lhpar = lhpar, sel_fun = sel_fun, ess.g = 200,
  settings = list(obs_model = "dm", CVL = 0.1,
                  sigmaF = 0.3,      # fixed (or the F_re estimate from the real data)
                  tail_cut = 47,     # absolute length, the same in every iteration
                  spr_ref = 40),
  spr = 40))
```

- `se = FALSE` is used inside `flicc.sa()`; fixed sigmaF avoids its estimation in
  every year and iteration.
- The tail cut and sigmaF both trade responsiveness against stability; tune them
  together with the smoothing of the harvest control rule.
- Expect the equilibrium model to be pessimistic during a rebuild and optimistic
  while F increases.

# Summary of checks and recommendations

| # | Check | Red flag | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | sample size by gear-year (`plot_lfdn`) | < 50 fish or < 10 bins; gear mix changing | ESS per gear; drop/pool poor gear-years |
| 2 | composition consistency (`plot_lfd`) | shifts in mode or left limb | split gears/periods; restrict years |
| 3 | largest fish vs Linf | > 1% at or above Linf | revisit Linf; tail cut |
| 4 | empirical catch curves (`plot_zlcc`) | curved limbs, jumping slopes | dome or tail cut; keep random walk |
| 5 | life-history inputs | Linf inconsistent with data; odd M/k | Linf sensitivity and ensemble |
| 6 | selectivity plausibility (`plot_sel`) | narrow or unsupported domes | logistic; fix from external data; dome sensitivity (`dome_sens_flicc`) |
| 7 | convergence (`flicc_convergence`) | gradient, Hessian, bounds | restarts; simplify; tail cut |
| 8 | fit to compositions (`plot_len`) | systematic misfit | selectivity, Linf, tail cut |
| 9 | retrospective | rho beyond ±0.2 | trends in selectivity or sampling |
| 10 | indicators vs status | gears disagree | best gear; pooling; HCR smoothing |

| Topic | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Observation model | `dm` with real data |
| Sample size | ESS about 150-200 per gear-year; never raw thousands |
| Growth | fix Linf and CVL; Linf is the main sensitivity; `maxsd = 3` as sensitivity |
| Selectivity | logistic unless supported; always run `dome_sens_flicc()` (rsd 1000 to 0.25 x Linf) |
| Management options | `plot_contour_flicc()`: yield and SPR (or SSB with `s`) over selectivity and F by gear |
| F over time | random walk, sigmaF fixed (0.3 or the `F_re` estimate) |
| Tail | `tail_cut` at about 0.80-0.85 x Linf, as a length |
| Missing data | keep zeros, rely on the random walk; not without random walk |
| Status | SPR at the year's F; `s` for $B/B_{tgt}$ under Beverton-Holt |
| Ensembles | ESS rescaled; CVL not drawn (`cv$CVL = 0`) and examined separately; tail cut; fixed sigmaF |
| MSE | fixed sigmaF, absolute tail cut, `se = FALSE`; tune with the HCR |

how SPR, the tail cut and sigmaF respond over time; estimated Dirichlet-multinomial
overdispersion.*
